name: Arrays & Hashing
analogy: A coat check takes your coat and hands you a ticket. Later you show the ticket and your coat comes back at once, with nobody searching the rack. A hash map is the same trade: spend a little memory and every lookup is instant.
whenToUse: You check the same values again and again
Counts, pairs or duplicates decide the answer
Brute force compares every pair of items

transcript.text: Which two numbers add to 9? Checking every pair, the answer only turns up on the tenth and last try. That is n² work.
Instead, walk the list once and keep a map of numbers you have seen. Each entry remembers a number and the index where it sits.
For each number, ask the map for its partner. At 5 you need 4, and 4 is already in the map, so the pair is 3 and 4.
One pass, one map lookup each: O(n) time. That’s arrays and hashing: memory traded for instant lookups.

name: Two Pointers
idea: Two indices walking toward an answer.
analogy: Two people start at opposite ends of a hallway and walk toward each other. Each step rules out a whole row of options they will never need to check. Two pointers prune a search the same way: every move discards what cannot win.
whenToUse: The input is sorted, or can be sorted first
You compare a pair from opposite ends
Each step rules out a whole row of options

transcript.text: Nine walls stand in a row, and you must pick the pair that holds the most water. Trying every pair means measuring 36 containers.
Instead, start with the widest container: the first and last walls. Measure what it holds.
The shorter wall is the limit, so move it inward. Moving the taller wall instead could never hold more.
Each wall moves at most once, so 8 measurements find the best: 49. That’s two pointers.

name: Sliding Window
idea: A range that grows and shrinks as it scans.
analogy: Look out of a train window. New scenery slides in on the right, old scenery slides out on the left, and you never re-read the whole view. You only deal with what changed.
whenToUse: The answer is a contiguous run (subarray or substring)
It asks for the longest, shortest or a count
Brute force is two nested loops

transcript.text: Say you need the longest stretch of a string with no repeated letters. The obvious way checks every start and every end: 36 windows for 8 letters.
Instead, keep a window. Move its right edge one letter at a time and remember what’s inside.
When a letter repeats, slide the left edge forward until the repeat is gone. The window never moves backwards.
Each letter enters once and leaves once. One pass, O(n). That’s the sliding window.

name: Stack
idea: Remember the past, answer on the way back.
analogy: Think of a stack of plates. You only ever touch the top one, and the last plate you put down is the first one you pick up.
whenToUse: The last thing seen must be handled first
Pairs nest inside each other, like brackets
You need to undo steps in reverse order

transcript.text: Six brackets, nested inside each other, and each closer must meet the right opener. Stripping pairs and rescanning reads the string again and again.
Instead, stack each opener as you read it. The stack remembers what is still waiting.
Each closer checks only the top plate, the newest opener still waiting. If they match, the pair is settled.
One pass, O(n) time. Empty stack, valid string. That’s the stack.

name: Binary Search
idea: Halve the search space every step.
analogy: Finding a word in a paper dictionary, you open near the middle and see which side the word falls on. The other half closes for good. Binary search works the same way: one comparison rules out half of what is left.
whenToUse: The input is sorted (or rotated sorted)
One check rules out half the input
You need log n, not a full scan

transcript.text: Seven numbers, sorted but rotated, and you need the smallest. Reading all seven works, but it touches every number.
Instead, compare the middle with the right end. That single check names the half holding the drop.
7 beats 2, so the drop sits right of mid. The left half goes, and the search space halves.
Halve again and again: O(log n). That’s binary search.

name: Linked List
idea: Rewire pointers without losing the chain.
analogy: A treasure hunt where each clue says where the next one hides. To run it backwards you rewrite one clue at a time, keeping a finger on the next clue before you overwrite it. Reversing a list is the same: save next, flip, step on.
whenToUse: Nodes link onward instead of sitting in a row
You rewire links without losing the chain
One pass with a few pointers is enough

transcript.text: Five nodes, each pointing at the next. You could copy the values into a new, backwards list, but that costs a new node for every old one.
Instead, walk the list with two pointers: prev behind, curr ahead. Nothing moves but the arrows.
For each node, save next first, then point curr back at prev. Never cut before you hold on.
One pass, O(n) time, and not a single new node. That’s the linked list.

name: Trees
analogy: A family tree spans as many generations as its longest branch. Each person asks their children how far down their lines run, then adds one for themselves. The root learns the whole height without ever seeing it.
whenToUse: Data branches into left and right children
Answers combine upward from the leaves
Each subtree looks like the whole tree

transcript.text: A tree with five nodes, and you need its depth. Walking every root-to-leaf path visits the shared nodes again and again.
Instead, ask each child how deep its side goes. An empty side answers 0, so a leaf answers 1.
20 hears 1 from each side, takes the deeper, adds one: 2. Answers bubble upward.
Each node answers once: O(n). The root says 3. That’s recursion on a tree.

name: Tries
idea: Share prefixes, find words letter by letter.
analogy: Start typing a word and your phone narrows the guesses with every letter. After two letters you are already on the right page for every word that starts that way. A trie stores words the same way, sharing each prefix once so a lookup only walks the letters you type.
whenToUse: The task is prefix search or autocomplete
Many words share the same beginnings
Lookups must cost one step per letter

transcript.text: Searching a word list means comparing the query with every word. “car”, “cat” and “cart” all start the same, so the same letters get read again and again.
A trie stores each shared beginning once. “car” and “cat” share c-a, then branch only where they differ.
Inserting reuses every node already there and marks where a word ends. Looking up “ca” walks c, then a, but no word ends there: search says no, startsWith says yes.
Each operation costs one hop per letter: O(L). That’s the trie.

name: Heaps
analogy: Picture a line of people sorted by height, split into two teams at the middle. The shorter team only watches its tallest member, and the taller team only its shortest. The median is always where the two teams meet, so nobody ever sorts the whole line.
whenToUse: Items arrive one at a time, unsorted
You need the middle, min or max so far
Brute force sorts after every arrival

transcript.text: Numbers arrive one at a time and you must report the median after each. Re-sorting everything so far after every number does the same work over and over.
Instead, split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half. Each half only watches the member closest to the split.
15 arrives and lands in the lower half, then the biggest of that half moves across. Both tops read 5 and 15, so the median is 10.
Each number costs one heap push and pop: O(log n). That’s the two-heap median.

name: Backtracking
analogy: Walk into a maze with a piece of chalk. When you hit a dead end, step back to the last fork and try the next turn, never walking the same dead end twice. Backtracking explores choices the same way, undoing each step so every option gets exactly one visit.
whenToUse: You must list every valid arrangement
Each step tries one of a few options
A wrong turn can be undone cleanly

transcript.text: Which sets of 2, 3, 6 and 7 add to 7? Trying every branch blindly means 28 nodes, most of them dead ends that overshoot.
Try one number at a time and carry what is left. Each choice narrows the question to a smaller target.
2, 2, 2 leaves only 1, and 2 is already too big, so that branch is cut. Back up: 2, 2 then 3 reaches exactly 7, so [2, 2, 3] is saved.
Trying every branch is exponential, but each cut prunes a whole subtree. That’s backtracking.

name: Graphs
idea: Explore neighbours with BFS and DFS.
analogy: Drop ink on any land square you have not coloured yet. It spreads to every square joined to it, but never crosses water. Each drop is one island, and counting the drops counts the islands.
whenToUse: The input is a grid or a network
Answers spread through neighbours
You must count joined-up regions

transcript.text: A grid of land and water hides joined-up islands. Flooding again from every land cell repeats the same ground over and over.
Scan row by row instead. The first unclaimed land, at row 0, col 0, must be a new island.
A queue floods from it to every joined square, claiming island 1. The scan moves on and finds two more.
Each cell is claimed once: O(m·n). Three drops of ink, three islands. That’s graph search.

name: Advanced Graphs
idea: Cheapest paths with Dijkstra, joined groups with Union-Find.
analogy: Ripples on a pond reach the closest shore first. Dijkstra works the same way: always finish the nearest place you know about, because nothing later can get there sooner. Union-Find is the other tool here: give every group one leader, and two people are in the same group when they name the same leader.
whenToUse: Roads have different costs
You want the cheapest or fastest route
Groups keep merging as links arrive

transcript.text: A signal leaves node 0 and the roads have different costs. Walking every route repeats the same roads again and again.
Keep a heap of arrival times. The smallest one can’t be beaten, so that node’s time is final.
Going through node 1 reaches node 2 at time 3, which beats the direct road of 4. A cheaper road updates the time.
Each road is checked once, so it’s O(E log V). The last node hears at time 7. That’s Dijkstra.

name: 1-D DP
analogy: Plan a route of jobs in a notebook, one line per day. Each line holds the best total so far, so tomorrow’s choice only looks at the last two lines. The final line is the answer, built without ever redoing a day.
whenToUse: Today’s answer builds on yesterday’s
Brute force retries the same subproblem
You only need the last few answers

transcript.text: Five houses hold 2, 7, 9, 3 and 1, but neighbours share an alarm. Trying all 32 sets of houses rechecks the same endings again and again.
Write down the best haul for the first house, then the first two. Each answer only needs the two cells before it.
At house 2, skipping keeps 7 but taking adds its 9 to 2. Taking wins, so dp[3] is 11.
One pass fills the row: O(n). The last cell reads 12, from houses 0, 2 and 4. That’s 1-D DP.

name: 2-D DP
idea: Fill a table cell by cell.
analogy: Picture a spreadsheet where every formula only points at the cells above and to the left. Fill it from the top-left corner and each cell becomes a small finished answer. The bottom-right cell then holds the whole answer, built without redoing a single cell.
whenToUse: Two strings or grids must be compared
Each answer builds on smaller prefixes
Brute force checks every pair of prefixes

transcript.text: “abcde” and “ace” share letters in order, but which run is longest? Listing every subsequence of “abcde” takes 32 checks, and it doubles with every letter.
Build a table instead. Each cell answers a smaller question: how much do these two prefixes share?
Fill it corner to corner. ‘c’ meets ‘c’, so take the diagonal 1 and add one: 2. A miss carries the best neighbour.
The corner reads 3: “ace”. One pass over the table, O(m·n) time. That’s 2-D DP.

name: Greedy
idea: Take the best move now. Never look back.
analogy: Cross a stream on stepping stones without ever planning the route. From each stone, only note the farthest stone you could land on. If the next stone sits past that mark, the crossing is impossible, and you knew without retracing a step.
whenToUse: A single choice now never needs revisiting
Only the best option so far matters
Brute force tries every combination

transcript.text: Five stones hold jumps of 2, 3, 1, 1 and 4. Can you reach the end? Trying every route means following the same jumps again and again.
Forget the route. Track one number instead: the farthest stone you could reach so far.
Stone 1 jumps 3, stretching the reach to 4, the end. Now try 3, 2, 1, 0, 4: the reach stalls at 3, so stone 4 is out of reach.
One scan, O(n) time: a stone past the reach means you’re stuck. That’s greedy: the best move now, never looking back.

name: Intervals
idea: Sort by start, then merge or split.
analogy: Lay every meeting of a shared day on one timeline in start order. Meetings that overlap or touch fuse into one busy block. What is left is the day’s true shape, with every gap visible.
whenToUse: Inputs are ranges with a start and end
Overlap or touching decides the answer
Order by start, then walk once

transcript.text: Four bookings cover 8–10, 1–3, 15–18 and 2–6. Which busy blocks do they really form? Comparing every pair means six checks.
Sort them by start instead. Once they line up, each booking only meets the block before it.
2–6 starts inside 1–3, so stretch the block to 1–6. 8–10 starts after 6, so it opens a new block.
One sort, one walk: O(n log n). Three blocks left: 1–6, 8–10 and 15–18. That’s intervals.

name: Math & Geometry
idea: Walk and transform grids with simple coordinates.
analogy: Peel an orange in one long strip: go around the outside, then around what’s left, and never touch the same skin twice. A grid works the same way. Four walls mark what’s left, and each side you walk pulls one wall in.
whenToUse: You must change a grid in place
The path follows the grid’s shape
A formula or flip replaces the simulation

transcript.text: Read this grid in a spiral, from the outside in. One way is a second grid that marks every cell you’ve seen. That’s 12 extra numbers.
You only need four walls: top, bottom, left and right. Everything between them is still unread.
Walk along one wall, then pull it in. The next side starts where the last one ended, and the box keeps shrinking.
Every cell is read once, so it’s O(m·n) time. Four walls are all the extra memory you need.

name: Bit Manipulation
idea: Use AND, XOR and shifts to work on single bits.
analogy: A number is a row of light switches. Binary tricks flip or read those switches directly. One trick turns off the rightmost lit switch in a single move, so counting the lit ones takes one move per light, and the dark ones are skipped.
whenToUse: The problem mentions bits or binary
Pairs cancel out (XOR)
You can’t use + or extra memory

transcript.text: 172 in binary is 10101100. Checking all eight bits works, but half of those checks land on zeros.
Think of a row of light switches. One trick turns off only the rightmost switch that’s lit.
Subtract one and the lowest 1 flips off. AND that with n, and only that one bit disappears.
Four 1 bits, four hops. That’s O(k) for k one bits, and the zeros are skipped.
